newsitem.title: UK: UK Tories in turmoil as Redwood backs Clarke.
newsitem.headline: UK Tories in turmoil as Redwood backs Clarke.

text.p: Kenneth Clarke dramatically boosted his chances of becoming leader of Britain's defeated Conservative party on Wednesday by joining forces with his erstwhile ideological foe over Europe, right-winger John Redwood.

But far from healing the divisions that led to the Conservatives' crushing defeat in the May 1 election, the extraordinary right-left alliance produced a furious tirade from former prime minister Margaret Thatcher.

"The Conservative party must rally round a position of principle -- not try to seek refuge in an incredible alliance of opposites, which can only lead to further grief," Thatcher, considered the standard bearer of the party's right wing, said in a statement.

She urged the main opposition party's 164 members of parliament to vote in Thursday's third and final leadership ballot for former Welsh secretary William Hague, the only rival to former finance minister Clarke.
"He (Hague) stands for the things I believe in -- above all, he offers a clear vision of Britain as a free, sovereign nation with control over its own affairs," she added.
Thatcher's statement was an allusion to Clarke's determination to keep open Britain's option about joining the European Union's planned single currency.

Redwood, forced by party rules to stand down after Tuesday's second round, has been just as fiercely opposed to economic and monetary union (EMU) in the past. He said his alliance with Clarke, finance minister under former prime minister John Major, did not mean he was abandoning his views.
In the unlikely event that Britain had to make up its mind about a single currency, Redwood said he would continue to speak out against scrapping the pound.

"I have agreed with Ken Clarke that my principled objections to a single currency will remain my position... There will be a free vote and the right for free speech on this issue should the matter arise at some point in the future," he said.

Clarke, with 64 votes, beat Hague by just two votes, leaving the outcome of Thursday's run-off vote in the hands of the 38 MPs who voted for Redwood. Several of them said publicly they would back Clarke, some others refused to be drawn.

Clarke, who said he would name Redwood his finance spokesman if he becomes leader, denied that they made strange bedfellows and produced a joint statement outlining the policies they would follow during the five-year life of the current parliament.

"The five-year deal is a deal with the whole Conservative party to fight as an effective opposition to get ourselves back into power," Clarke said. "What we've got to do is respect each other's opinions and convictions."
Redwood said he wanted an "honourable peace" with Clarke to end the party's civil war.
"I said we needed to stop the Balkanisation of the party with little groups in little cells in little corners and little rooms arguing through the media with each other," he said.

Redwood was thrust into the role of kingmaker in the contest to succeed former prime minister John Major after he was eliminated in Tuesday's second ballot, when he trailed in third behind Clarke and Hague, just 36.
Hague's backers dubbed the Clarke-Redwood ticket an "instability pact", but Clarke said there was a strong desire among Conservative activists for the party to pull together.
"People will welcome that the party is coming to its senses and getting down to the serious task of producing a body of policies," he said.

Hague lost support from many MPs after ruling out joining a single currency last week. This was seen as an attempt to appease Euro-sceptics and Hague further annoyed Conservatives by saying no one who opposed his new line would find a place in any "shadow" cabinet he formed.
